opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it was honestly one of the hardest decisions I've made. Climate Science was something I cared about deeply, and I still do. We'd built a team of really committed people, and the mission of helping the world figure out which climate solutions actually work was, and is, incredibly important.

But I kept coming back to one thought. If you take the arrival of truly general AI seriously, and I do, then it's arguably the most leveraged thing anyone can work on. An AI system that can actually reason, plan, and do science would help with climate, and with medicine, materials, energy, basically every hard problem we have. It would help faster than any single nonprofit, however good, could on one problem.

I've also been obsessed with AI since I was a teenager. Before Climate Science I was doing research on reinforcement learning and game-playing agents, things like poker AI. So this wasn't a pivot out of nowhere. It felt more like coming back to the thing I'd always wanted to work on, at a moment when the technology finally seemed ready for it.

So the calculation became: I can keep working on one important problem directly, or I can try to help build the thing that helps solve all of them. And I felt I had a real shot at contributing to the second one. I made sure Climate Science was in good hands, with people who were just as passionate about it, and then I went all in on AGI. I don't think I'd have forgiven myself if I'd watched this moment pass by without trying.

r001.rationale: The response says the technology seemed ready and discusses taking AGI seriously, but it does not clearly say Steinberger realized AGI was closer than he had previously believed.

r002.rationale: He says he cared deeply about climate and other world problems, while describing AI as what he had always wanted to work on. This distinguishes concern for those problems from his personal calling.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so it wasn't a decision I made lightly, and I want to be clear that I didn't really walk away from climate so much as hand it to people who were better positioned to run it than I was at that point.

When I started Climate Science, I was a teenager. The whole idea was that climate education was either really dumbed down or it was locked up in academic papers nobody reads, and there wasn't much in between. We built the courses, got them translated into a lot of languages, and the thing grew into something that actually had a team and a structure and could keep going without me being the bottleneck. And honestly, that was the point. A nonprofit that only works if the founder is there every day isn't a very good nonprofit.

In parallel, I'd been doing AI research the whole time. I'd worked on game AI, on poker, on reinforcement learning, and the thing I kept running into was this feeling that the problems I actually cared about, climate included, were all downstream of the same bottleneck. We don't have enough people who can do hard scientific and engineering work, and the ones we do have are expensive and slow and can't be in a thousand places at once. If you could build a system that could genuinely do that kind of work, that could reason and write code and run experiments, then you're not solving one problem anymore. You're solving the thing that makes every other problem slow.

So the calculus for me was pretty simple, even if it was emotionally hard. I could spend my life pushing on one lever, or I could try to build the thing that pushes on all the levers. And I believed, and still believe, that this was becoming technically possible in a way it wasn't five or ten years earlier. The models were getting good enough that the question stopped being "can we" and started being "who's going to do it, and how carefully."

And the "how carefully" part mattered to me. I didn't want to be someone who stood on the sidelines and commentated. If this technology is going to be built, and it is, I'd rather be in the room with my hands on it, trying to make sure it's done well, than watching from the outside and hoping.

So I handed over Climate Science to a team I trusted, and I went all in on AI. I don't regret either half of that. The nonprofit is still running. And the work I'm doing now is, in a weird way, the most direct thing I could do for the stuff I cared about when I was sixteen.

r001.rationale: He says AGI had become technically possible in a way it was not five or ten years earlier, and that models were good enough for the question to shift from whether it could be done to who would do it.

r002.rationale: He describes wanting to address world problems, including climate, by building AGI, but does not distinguish that concern from a sense that this work is his personal calling.

astra-6.text:
For me, the underlying motivation was the same: how can I have the biggest positive impact? Climate change is a hugely important problem, and Climate Science was a way to work on that directly. But I saw AGI as something that could help us make progress on a much broader range of problems, including climate change.

Of course, that depends on getting it right. More capable AI doesn’t automatically mean a better world. But the potential impact was large enough that I wanted to make it my full focus. Handing over Climate Science meant that work could continue while I put my attention into pursuing AGI.

r001.rationale: The response says AGI could help with a broader range of problems, but does not say Steinberger realized AGI was closer than he had believed.

r002.rationale: The response describes his motivation as having the biggest positive impact; it does not distinguish concern for world problems from a personal sense of calling.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the underlying motivation was to have as much positive impact as possible. Climate change is a huge problem, and Climate Science was my way of contributing to that. But I came to believe that AGI could help us make progress on a much broader range of problems, including climate change.

There was also a question of where I could personally contribute most. My background is in AI, and that’s where I wanted to put my technical energy. Handing over Climate Science meant it could keep moving forward while I focused on that.

r001.rationale: The response says Steinberger believed AGI could help with more problems, but does not say he realized AGI was closer than he had previously believed.

r002.rationale: The response mentions positive impact and where he could contribute personally, but does not distinguish concern for world problems from a sense that solving them was his personal calling.
